strengths: Originality and significance: The paper identifies a useful, specific incentive problem in LLM billing: providers can increase reported token counts while preserving the delivered text. Connecting tokenization ambiguity to pricing incentives is an interesting contribution.

Methodological merits: The principal-agent formulation makes the restricted manipulation explicit. Under string-preserving deviations and additive pricing, the characterization of tokenization-invariant prices as sums of character prices is intuitive and useful.

Empirical evidence: Experiments cover five models across three families, multiple sampling settings, and five repetitions. They demonstrate that longer tokenizations satisfying top-p support constraints can exist in practice, with reported billing increases reaching approximately 13%.

Presentation and ethics: The paper is generally clearly organized, includes algorithm pseudocode and experimental details, and explicitly discusses misuse, assumptions, and dataset limitations. Its treatment of the attack as a vulnerability demonstration is reasonable.
weaknesses: Soundness—undetectability is not established. Equation 3 checks only whether every token belongs to the relevant top-p support. This does not establish that manipulated sequences have typical likelihoods or evade statistical detection across requests. No detection experiment supports the repeated claim that providers can overcharge 'without raising suspicion.' Section 5 acknowledges this distinction, but the abstract and conclusions remain stronger than the evidence.

Soundness—the incentive-compatibility definition contradicts the main pricing theorem as written. Definition 4 quantifies over all reported sequences, without requiring preservation of the generated string. Together with Equation 1, this requires equal rewards for every sequence; positive pay-per-character pricing fails because reporting a longer string increases payment. Restricting deviations to the same string would repair the intended statement, but this restriction must appear in the formal definition and theorem.

Soundness—the probability-threshold hardness extension has a proof gap. Appendix B.1.2, Equation 9 bounds a non-Hamiltonian sequence by delta times a probability factor raised to n−1, although alternative tokenizations need not contain n tokens. Shorter sequences containing an invalid transition can exceed the proposed threshold. The construction also leaves the initial distribution unspecified and assigns zero probability to the purported original single-token output. This extension needs a corrected reduction.

Economic evidence: The measured outcome is additional billed tokens, not net profit. Section 3.3 treats a full-sequence verification pass as negligible without latency, energy, or cost measurements. A single parallel forward pass still incurs computation, including on unsuccessful attempts. This omission is consequential when reported gains fall to 0.3% at p=0.9.

Significance and evaluation scope: The strongest empirical results use permissive sampling, especially temperature 1.3 and p=0.99. The experiments use only 400 short English prompts and outputs of 200–300 tokens; there is no systematic heuristic evaluation at temperature 1.0 or below. These results support a conditional vulnerability demonstration, but not the broad practical conclusions about current services. Likewise, worst-case NP-hardness for constructed next-token distributions does not establish a practical computational barrier for deployed models.

Reproducibility: Appendix A specifies hardware, models, filtering, and broad generation settings, but provides no code link, exact seeds, software versions, chat-template configuration, or precise output-length controls. The stated t critical value of 2.015 also does not match a two-sided 90% interval with four degrees of freedom from five repetitions. These omissions and inconsistencies hinder independent verification.

strengths: Originality and significance: The paper identifies a useful economic consequence of nonunique output tokenization: providers can increase reported token counts while preserving the delivered text. Connecting this ambiguity to billing incentives is a worthwhile perspective.

Methodology: Algorithm 1 is simple and clearly specified. Experiments across five models from three families demonstrate that longer tokenizations can remain within top-p sampling support, providing evidence for the restricted vulnerability studied.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is generally readable, with helpful examples, pseudocode, and appendix proofs. Appendix A specifies hardware, model repositories, prompt filtering, and repeated generations.

Limitations and ethics: Section 5 candidly discusses restricted pricing assumptions, proprietary-model coverage, other provider manipulations, and possible misuse. The defensive motivation and explicit misuse discussion are appropriate; no material ethical deficiency is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central claims exceed the evidence: Membership in top-p support establishes that a sequence is possible, not that manipulation occurs 'without raising suspicion.' Repeatedly choosing longer tokenizations can alter observable token frequencies and likelihoods. No statistical detection experiment supports the undetectability claim. Furthermore, provider-supplied probabilities require a trust or verification assumption; disclosing them alone does not establish their authenticity. Section 5 acknowledges these issues, but the abstract and conclusions remain substantially stronger than the results.

Soundness—incorrect incentive-compatibility statement: Definition 4 quantifies over every reported sequence, without requiring preservation of the output string. Under Equation 1, applying this definition in both directions forces all sequences to receive the same reward. Positive pay-per-character pricing therefore does not satisfy the stated definition, contrary to Theorem 6. Restricting deviations to sequences with the same string would repair the intended characterization, but this restriction must appear explicitly in the definition and theorem.

Soundness—an appendix hardness proof is incomplete: In Appendix B.1.2, Equation 9 bounds a non-Hamiltonian tokenization's probability using n factors. However, alternative tokenizations of the target string need not contain n tokens: repeated longer tokens can produce shorter sequences. One low-probability transition therefore does not imply the displayed bound, and the stated condition on delta does not resolve this. The claimed extension to a sequence-probability threshold needs a corrected reduction. Separately, the worst-case hardness result does not establish practical difficulty for deployed LLM distributions.

Economic evidence: The experiments measure additional billed tokens, not net profit. Section 3.3 calls verification cost negligible because it requires one forward pass, but scoring an entire modified sequence still incurs computation and memory costs. No latency, energy, or cost measurements establish that the extra revenue exceeds this overhead, particularly where reported overcharging is only 0.3–2.6%. The generation-only utility model omits precisely this attack cost.

Evaluation and significance: The headline 13% result occurs at temperature 1.3 and p=0.99; gains fall sharply at lower p. Appendix C evaluates temperatures 1.15–1.45, leaving the heuristic's behavior at temperature 1 or below insufficiently documented. Evaluation also uses only 400 short English prompts and outputs of 200–300 tokens. These results support a specialized proof of concept, but not the manuscript's broad practical conclusions about current services.

Reproducibility and technical precision: No implementation link, exact seeds, package versions, or complete generation configuration is provided. Appendix A uses a t critical value of 2.015 for five repetitions; a two-sided 90% interval with four degrees of freedom requires approximately 2.132. The assumption that every character is an individual vocabulary token also needs reconciliation with byte-based tokenization, Unicode, and special tokens before the character-level claims can be applied generally.

Scope of the proposed remedy: The pricing characterization is useful under additive prices and fixed-string deviations, but broader uniqueness language obscures these restrictions. Other string-dependent pricing rules are invariant to retokenization when additivity is relaxed. The paper also does not compare character pricing with billing a deterministic, publicly specified retokenization of the delivered text, which could remove the same reporting ambiguity while retaining token-based units.

strengths: Originality and significance: The paper identifies a useful connection between nonunique output tokenization and provider incentives under per-token billing. Studying manipulation that preserves the delivered text is a focused contribution distinct from model-substitution attacks.

Methodology: The fixed-string model clearly explains why reporting longer tokenizations increases revenue. Under the intended restriction to string-preserving reports, character-based additive pricing provides a simple, verifiable remedy. The Hamiltonian-path reduction also offers an interesting worst-case perspective.

Evaluation: Experiments cover five models from three families, 400 prompts, and five repetitions. Figure 2 demonstrates that longer tokenizations satisfying the specified top-p constraints exist in practice, with overcharging reaching approximately 13% in one evaluated setting.

Presentation and ethics: The manuscript is generally readable, provides pseudocode and experimental details, and openly discusses restricted assumptions, dataset representativeness, implementation barriers, and potential misuse. The limitations and broader-impact discussion are constructive.
weaknesses: Soundness—plausibility does not establish undetectability: Equation 3 only requires each reported token to belong to the relevant top-p support. This does not establish that manipulated sequences have typical likelihoods or that repeated reports evade statistical detection. No detection experiment is provided. Consequently, the repeated claim that providers can overcharge 'without raising suspicion' exceeds the demonstrated result. The proposed audit also needs a clearer trust model: provider-supplied probabilities are not independently authenticated, and an individual token's probability alone does not determine top-p membership.

Soundness—financial profitability is unverified: Section 3.3 calls the attack cost negligible because plausibility can be checked in one forward pass, but a pass over an entire modified response still requires substantial computation. There are no timing, memory, energy, or net-profit measurements. This is material because Figure 2 reports gains of only about 0.3% at p=0.9 and 1.6–2.6% at p=0.95. Additional billed tokens establish increased revenue, not increased profit.

Formal correctness: Definition 4 quantifies over every reported sequence, without requiring its string to equal the generated string. Taken literally, it forces all sequences to have the same reward, contradicting positive per-character pricing in Theorem 6. The intended restriction is explained earlier and would repair this issue, but the central theorem is false as formally stated. Separately, Appendix B.1.2's Equation 9 assumes an n-token probability product even though a non-Hamiltonian tokenization may contain fewer than n tokens; one low-probability transition therefore does not establish the claimed bound. That hardness extension needs a corrected reduction.

Significance and empirical scope: The principal attack results use temperatures above 1, with the largest highlighted gains occurring at temperature 1.3 and p=0.99. Comparable attack results at temperature 1 or below are missing. The short English prompts and outputs restricted to 200–300 tokens further limit generalization. These experiments support an existence demonstration under selected settings, rather than the manuscript's broad practical vulnerability claims.

Theoretical scope and originality: The hardness result concerns worst-case constructed next-token distributions; it does not establish computational difficulty for deployed LLMs. Likewise, the pricing characterization relies on additive rewards, availability of single-character tokens, and fixed output strings. It is a useful observation, but its uniqueness and incentive-compatibility claims should remain explicitly confined to that setting.

Reproducibility: Appendix A supplies hardware, model sources, filtering rules, and repeated-generation counts, but no implementation release is identified, and exact seeds, package versions, chat templates, and length-control settings are missing. The stated t multiplier of 2.015 also does not match a two-sided 90% interval estimated from five repetitions, which has four degrees of freedom. These gaps, together with the unsupported detection and profitability claims, prevent acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Originality and significance: The paper identifies a useful connection between nonunique output tokenizations and provider billing incentives. Preserving the exact output string distinguishes this manipulation from hidden-reasoning inflation and model substitution.

Soundness: Under the stated assumptions of additive pricing, string-preserving reports, and zero GPU cost for some reporting policies, Proposition 5 and Theorem 6 provide a clear characterization of incentive-compatible prices through character counts. The resulting pricing prescription is simple and actionable within this model.

Empirical merits: Experiments cover five models from three families, vary sampling parameters, and report repeated-run uncertainty. Algorithm 2 demonstrates that longer tokenizations can remain within the model's sampling support. The multilingual analysis also usefully exposes variation in provider margins.

Presentation and ethics: The manuscript is generally readable, with explicit definitions, pseudocode, and illustrative examples. It appropriately acknowledges potential misuse, verbosity incentives, proprietary-model limitations, and uncertainty about the prompt distribution.
weaknesses: Soundness of the central detectability claim: Membership in every top-p set establishes possibility, not statistical indistinguishability. Algorithm 2 can systematically distort the distribution of reported tokenizations while satisfying this constraint. No auditing experiment or distributional analysis supports the repeated claim that overcharging occurs 'without raising suspicion.' The limitations discussion acknowledges statistical auditing, but the abstract and conclusions still overstate the evidence.

Financial significance is insufficiently established beyond the simplified energy model. Section 3.3 treats verification cost as constant based on short-sequence measurements and evaluates profitability using GPU electricity costs and hypothetical margins. It does not measure end-to-end attack overhead or account for throughput, batching, and hardware opportunity costs. Figure 11's shared scale also makes verification-cost variation difficult to assess. These omissions matter particularly when reported revenue gains are below a few percent.

Theoretical claims need correction and tighter scope. Appendix B.1.2, Eq. 10 bounds an invalid tokenization's probability using n-1 high-probability factors, although alternative tokenizations can contain fewer than n tokens. A shorter sequence containing a low-probability transition can therefore exceed the proposed threshold; the stated reduction does not establish this extension. Separately, Theorem 3 concerns constructed next-token distributions and worst-case complexity, which does not justify language suggesting providers using practical fixed models are generally 'likely to fail.'

Evaluation coverage limits the broad deployment claims. The attack experiments use temperatures 1.15, 1.30, and 1.45, short prompts of 20–100 characters, and outputs of 200–300 tokens. They do not establish effectiveness at temperature 1 or below, or in longer-context production workloads. Figure 3 also uses the optimal iteration count selected from the same prompts in Figure 2, without a held-out assessment of that choice.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Footnote 3 ends with 'The code we used in our experiments is available at' but supplies no link. Appendix A says every experiment uses an A100, whereas Figure 11 and Table 1 specify an H100 for the energy measurements that underpin profitability. Exact software versions, sampled prompt identifiers, and seeds are also absent.

The pricing recommendation needs clearer economic interpretation. Section 4's calibration preserves the unweighted average of per-output profit margins under a stable output distribution; it need not preserve aggregate profit or the revenue-weighted business margin. Moreover, uniqueness applies only within additive pricing and the restricted string-preserving manipulation model. The contribution remains useful, but broader claims about eliminating provider incentives and maintaining profitability should retain these qualifications.

strengths: Originality and significance: The paper identifies a useful connection between ambiguous output tokenization and provider incentives. Preserving the output string distinguishes this vulnerability from model substitution and injected reasoning tokens discussed in related work.

Soundness: Under the stated restrictions to additive prices and string-preserving reporting, Proposition 5 and Theorem 6 provide a coherent characterization of incentive-compatible pricing. The character-price calibration also correctly preserves the expected per-output profit margin under the assumed cost model and a stable output distribution.

Evaluation: Experiments span five models from three families, include repeated generations, and measure GPU energy rather than simply equating extra revenue with profit. The results establish that longer, top-p-compatible tokenizations can occur in the tested settings.

Presentation and ethics: The motivation, algorithms, and economic model are generally understandable. Section 5 appropriately acknowledges unverifiable probability reports, verbosity incentives, dataset limitations, and potential misuse of the attack. These are valuable disclosures.
weaknesses: Soundness—undetectability is not established: Membership in each top-p set establishes that a sequence is possible, not that strategic reporting is statistically indistinguishable from truthful generation. Algorithm 2 systematically changes the output distribution, but no detection experiment or statistical guarantee supports the repeated claim of overcharging 'without raising suspicion.' Moreover, provider-reported probabilities are not independently authenticated. Section 5 acknowledges these issues, but the abstract and conclusions still exceed the evidence.

Soundness—the probability-threshold hardness extension contains an invalid step: Appendix B.1.2, Eq. 10 bounds a non-Hamiltonian tokenization by δ((1−δ)/n)^(n−1), implicitly assuming it has n tokens. Repeated long tokens can represent the target string with fewer tokens. For n=3, the target has six characters and ('aaa','aaa') has only two tokens. Taking the permitted δ=0.2 and the intended first-token probability (1−δ)/3 gives probability approximately 0.0533, exceeding the proposed threshold approximately 0.0190 despite repeating a vertex. The converse reduction therefore does not follow as written.

Soundness and practical significance—the profitability claim rests on a narrow cost approximation: Section 3.3 treats verification cost as independent of sequence length and uses GPU energy alone to establish financial gain. Appendix C.3 measures a limited length range on an isolated GPU; it does not establish constant verification cost more generally or account for serving throughput, batching, latency, and the complete reporting procedure. These measurements support a conditional energy-based result, but not the broader operational profitability claim.

Evaluation—the strongest attack results concern permissive sampling: The attack experiments use temperatures 1.15–1.45, with 1.3 in the main figures. For Llama-3.2-1B, reported overcharging falls from 11.2% at p=0.99 to 1.8% at p=0.95 and 0.28% at p=0.90. Results at temperature 1 or below are needed to establish reach beyond the highlighted high-temperature setting. The iteration budget is also selected from the reported evaluation curves without a separate tuning/test evaluation.

Theoretical scope: The main hardness construction concerns specially constructed prefix-dependent distributions and vocabularies. Worst-case NP-hardness does not establish that finding optimal attacks against the evaluated, fixed LLMs is practically difficult. Statements that a provider is 'likely to fail' require qualification; the manuscript provides neither typical-case evidence nor a demonstrated computational barrier for these models.

Significance—the pricing recommendation needs a stronger comparison: The uniqueness result depends on additivity over reported tokens. A contract charging according to a publicly specified canonical tokenization of the returned string is also invariant to reported segmentation, although outside that additive class. Comparing this directly with pay-per-character would clarify the practical necessity of changing billing units. Also, preserving the unweighted mean of per-output margins does not generally preserve aggregate profit or aggregate revenue margin.

Reproducibility and presentation: The code-availability footnote on page 3 ends without a link. Appendix A states that every experiment uses an A100, whereas Appendix C.3 identifies an H100 for energy measurements. Exact software versions, seeds, and generation-length controls are missing, and duplicated model labels create further ambiguity. These issues matter particularly because the financial conclusions depend on small measured verification costs.

strengths: Originality: The paper identifies a useful connection between nonunique output tokenization and provider billing incentives. This is meaningfully distinct from the discussed work on model substitution and hidden reasoning tokens.

Soundness: Under the stated restriction to string-preserving reports, additive pricing, and zero-GPU-cost reporting policies, Proposition 5 and Theorem 6 provide a clean characterization of incentive-compatible pricing. The pay-per-character prescription is simple and actionable within this model.

Significance: The experiments demonstrate that plausible alternative tokenizations can increase billed token counts across several model families. For example, Section 3.3 reports 11.2% additional tokens for Llama-3.2-1B at temperature 1.3 and top-p = 0.99. This establishes a concrete vulnerability worth studying.

Presentation and ethics: The manuscript is generally clear, with explicit definitions, readable algorithms, and helpful examples. Section 5 candidly discusses statistical auditing, verbosity incentives, market-level limitations, and potential misuse. The multilingual margin analysis adds useful context, and I see no unresolved material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness of the central detection claim: Membership in every top-p sampling set establishes possibility, not statistical indistinguishability from honest generation. Algorithm 2 systematically changes the distribution of reported tokenizations, potentially leaving detectable evidence even when every token is plausible. No auditing experiment or detection bound supports the repeated claim that providers can overcharge 'without raising suspicion.' Section 5 acknowledges statistical auditing, but the abstract and conclusions still overstate what the experiments establish.

Profitability evidence is narrower than the claims: Equation 4 and Figure 3 use a GPU-energy-only utility model and an approximately constant verification cost. Appendix C.3 measures short sequences on an isolated GPU; this does not establish length-independent verification costs generally or profitability under batched serving, where generation efficiency, GPU capacity, and latency matter. The manuscript should either narrow its financial claims to the measured setting or evaluate realistic serving costs and sensitivity to these assumptions.

Technical gap in Appendix B.1.2: Equation 10 bounds a non-Hamiltonian tokenization's probability by δ((1−δ)/n)^(n−1), implicitly assuming at least n tokens. Alternative tokenizations of the same string can contain fewer than n tokens through repetition of longer tokens, so one low-probability transition need not push their total probability below ε. The initial-token distribution is also unspecified. Consequently, the claimed extension to sequence-probability thresholds is not established by the supplied proof.

Scope of the hardness result: Theorem 3 uses a constructed, graph-dependent next-token rule and establishes worst-case hardness. It does not establish that optimal retokenization is difficult for the deployed LLMs studied experimentally. The language that transparent providers are 'likely to fail' at optimization goes beyond this result; the computational representation of the next-token rule should also be specified.

Empirical coverage limits practical significance: The attack evaluation emphasizes temperatures above 1, short English prompts, and outputs of 200–300 tokens. Gains depend strongly on sampling parameters: the highlighted Llama result drops from 11.2% at top-p = 0.99 to 0.28% at 0.90. Results at temperature 1 and below, broader output lengths, and held-out selection of the split count would better establish practical reach. A comparison with billing based on a publicly specified canonical retokenization would also clarify the need for changing the billing unit.

Reproducibility: The code-availability footnote on page 3 contains no URL. Appendix A states that every experiment uses an A100, whereas Figure 11 and Table 1 specify an H100; this discrepancy directly affects the cost evidence. Exact software versions, numerical precision, batching configuration, and energy-measurement details are insufficiently specified. These issues, together with the unsupported detection claim and proof gap, prevent acceptance despite the promising core idea.
